scheme.title: Teaching meta-processes
scheme.description: The processes that sit under teaching: planning learning, delivering it, evaluating it and reflecting on all three. Written for early career educators.
scheme.note: The base URI is a placeholder. Replace it with a namespace your institution controls before publishing.

concepts.label: Teaching cycle
concepts.def: The repeating loop in which planning shapes delivery, delivery produces evidence, evaluation interprets that evidence and the result changes the next plan.
concepts.scope: Use the term for the whole loop. Use Planning learning, Delivering learning, Evaluating learning or Reflective practice when you mean one part of it.
concepts.example: A librarian notices in a workshop that learners cannot find a database, then moves that step earlier in next term's plan.
concepts.source: Kolb, D.A. (1984) Experiential learning. Englewood Cliffs: Prentice Hall.

concepts.label: Planning learning
concepts.def: Deciding what learners should be able to do, what evidence will show it and which activities will get them there, before the session starts.
concepts.scope: Covers the decisions made before teaching. Decisions made during a session belong to Delivering learning.
concepts.example: Writing the outcome, the check for it and the first activity before choosing any slides.

concepts.label: Delivering learning
concepts.def: Running a session so that learners meet new material, practise it and show you what they understand, while you adjust to what you see.
concepts.scope: Covers what happens in the room or online. It includes the small decisions that no plan can settle in advance.
concepts.example: Pausing an explanation to ask learners to write one sentence in their own words.

concepts.label: Evaluating learning
concepts.def: Gathering evidence about what learners learned and how well the teaching supported it, then judging both against the intended outcomes.
concepts.scope: Covers judging learners' work and judging the teaching. The two are linked but they are not the same task.
concepts.example: Comparing exit-ticket answers with the session outcome to see which part needs re-teaching.

concepts.label: Reflective practice
concepts.def: Thinking deliberately about your own teaching, during and after it, so that what you learn changes what you do next.
concepts.scope: Reflection is more than reviewing whether a session went well. It ends in a decision about practice.
concepts.example: Writing three sentences after a session that end with one change you will make.
concepts.source: Schön, D.A. (1983) The reflective practitioner: how professionals think in action. New York: Basic Books.

concepts.label: Evidence of learning
concepts.def: Anything observable that shows what a learner knows or can do, such as an answer, a draft, a question or a performance.
concepts.scope: Evidence is not the same as impressions. A quiet room is not evidence of understanding.
concepts.example: A learner's one-sentence summary written at the end of a demonstration.

concepts.label: Learning outcome
concepts.def: A statement of what a learner will be able to do by the end of a session or course, written so that someone could observe it.
concepts.scope: Start with an action verb the learner performs. Avoid verbs such as understand or know, which you cannot observe.
concepts.example: Reference a journal article correctly in a short paragraph using the department style.
concepts.source: Biggs, J. (1996) Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32(3), pp. 347-364.

concepts.label: Cognitive taxonomy
concepts.def: A classification of thinking from remembering and understanding through applying, analysing, evaluating and creating, used to pitch an outcome at the right level.
concepts.scope: Use it to check that outcomes and tasks ask for the same kind of thinking. It is a planning aid, not a ladder learners must climb in order.
concepts.example: Changing an outcome from describe to compare once learners already know the basic terms.
concepts.source: Anderson, L.W. and Krathwohl, D.R. (eds.) (2001) A taxonomy for learning, teaching and assessing. New York: Longman.

concepts.label: Backward design
concepts.def: Planning in three steps: identify the intended results, decide what evidence would show them, then choose the activities that lead there.
concepts.scope: It reverses the habit of starting from a topic or a favourite activity. The activity comes last.
concepts.example: Deciding that learners will draft a search strategy, then planning the practice that prepares them to do it.
concepts.source: Wiggins, G. and McTighe, J. (2005) Understanding by design. 2nd edn. Alexandria, VA: ASCD.

concepts.label: Constructive alignment
concepts.def: Designing outcomes, learning activities and assessment so that all three point at the same thing, and learners build understanding by doing the activities.
concepts.scope: Check it by asking of each activity and each assessment task which outcome it serves. A mismatch is a design fault, not a learner fault.
concepts.example: An outcome asks learners to critique sources, so the activity and the check both require critiquing, not listing.
concepts.source: Biggs, J. (1996) Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32(3), pp. 347-364.

concepts.label: Prior knowledge
concepts.def: What learners already know, believe or can do when the session begins, including ideas that are wrong or incomplete.
concepts.scope: Find out before you plan the detail. Prior knowledge decides where you start and how much support you need.
concepts.example: A two-question poll before the session showing that half the group has never used a thesaurus search.
concepts.source: Ambrose, S.A., Bridges, M.W., DiPietro, M., Lovett, M.C. and Norman, M.K. (2010) How learning works: seven research-based principles for smart teaching. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

concepts.label: Session sequencing
concepts.def: Arranging the parts of a session in an order that builds each step on the one before: review, new material, guided practice, independent practice.
concepts.scope: A sequence is a hypothesis about how learners will move. Plan where you will check that it holds.
concepts.example: Starting with a short recap question, then a demonstration, then paired practice.
concepts.source: Rosenshine, B. (2012) Principles of instruction: research-based strategies that all teachers should know. American Educator, 36(1), pp. 12-19.

concepts.label: Cognitive load
concepts.def: The demand a task places on working memory, which can hold only a few new items at once.
concepts.scope: Too much new material, or a confusing layout, leaves no capacity for learning. Cut or split material before you add support.
concepts.example: Splitting a seven-step search method into two parts with a practice task between them.
concepts.source: Sweller, J. (1988) Cognitive load during problem solving: effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), pp. 257-285.

concepts.label: Scaffolding
concepts.def: Temporary support that lets a learner complete a task they could not manage alone, withdrawn as their competence grows.
concepts.scope: Plan how and when the support goes. Support that never leaves can stop learners building independence.
concepts.example: A sentence starter on the first attempt, a bare prompt on the second, nothing on the third.
concepts.source: Wood, D., Bruner, J.S. and Ross, G. (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2), pp. 89-100.

concepts.label: Active learning
concepts.def: Learning in which learners do something with the material, such as solving, explaining, comparing or making, and think about what they are doing.
concepts.scope: Being busy is not enough. The task must require the thinking the outcome names.
concepts.example: Pairs ranking three search strategies and justifying the order.
concepts.source: Freeman, S., Eddy, S.L., McDonough, M., Smith, M.K., Okoroafor, N., Jordt, H. and Wenderoth, M.P. (2014) Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(23), pp. 8410-8415.

concepts.label: Inclusive design
concepts.def: Planning for the range of learners you are likely to have by offering more than one way to engage with, receive and show learning, instead of adapting after a barrier appears.
concepts.scope: Start by asking where a barrier could arise in your plan. Offer choices that all reach the same outcome.
concepts.example: Giving key instructions in writing as well as aloud, and allowing a spoken or written answer.
concepts.source: CAST (2018) Universal Design for Learning Guidelines version 2.2. Available at: https://udlguidelines.cast.org (Accessed: 20 October 2026).

concepts.label: Explaining
concepts.def: Presenting new material in small, ordered steps, often with a worked example, so that learners can follow the reasoning and not only the answer.
concepts.scope: Say your thinking aloud. Stop at natural points to check what has landed.
concepts.example: Working through one search strategy on screen while naming each decision.
concepts.source: Rosenshine, B. (2012) Principles of instruction: research-based strategies that all teachers should know. American Educator, 36(1), pp. 12-19.

concepts.label: Questioning
concepts.def: Using questions to find out what learners think and to make them think, rather than only to test whether they know the answer.
concepts.scope: Allow thinking time. Ask every learner to commit to an answer before you take one.
concepts.example: Asking everyone to write a prediction before showing the result.
concepts.source: Black, P. and Wiliam, D. (1998) Inside the black box: raising standards through classroom assessment. London: King's College London.

concepts.label: Checking for understanding
concepts.def: Gathering quick evidence from all learners during teaching about whether they have grasped the point, so that you know whether to move on.
concepts.scope: A check must reach every learner. Asking whether there are any questions rarely does.
concepts.example: Mini-whiteboards, a one-question poll or a one-sentence written summary.
concepts.source: Wiliam, D. (2011) Embedded formative assessment. Bloomington, IN: Solution Tree Press.

concepts.label: Retrieval practice
concepts.def: Asking learners to recall material from memory instead of rereading it, which strengthens later recall.
concepts.scope: Keep it low stakes. Space it out and return to earlier material.
concepts.example: Opening a session with three questions about last week's content.
concepts.source: Roediger, H.L. and Karpicke, J.D. (2006) Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), pp. 249-255.

concepts.label: Responsive teaching
concepts.def: Changing what you do during a session because of the evidence you have just gathered, for example by re-explaining, speeding up or regrouping learners.
concepts.scope: Decide in advance what you will do if a check shows the group has not understood.
concepts.example: Replacing a planned task with a second worked example after a poll shows most learners are unsure.
concepts.source: Black, P. and Wiliam, D. (2009) Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educational Assessment, Evaluation and Accountability, 21(1), pp. 5-31.

concepts.label: Learning climate
concepts.def: The conditions in a session that make it likely learners will contribute, make mistakes in the open and ask for help.
concepts.scope: Climate is built by routines and responses, such as how you treat a wrong answer. It is not a matter of personality.
concepts.example: Saying that a wrong first attempt is useful data and then using it.
concepts.source: Ambrose, S.A., Bridges, M.W., DiPietro, M., Lovett, M.C. and Norman, M.K. (2010) How learning works: seven research-based principles for smart teaching. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

concepts.label: Pacing
concepts.def: Managing the time given to each part of a session so that the important parts get the time they need and the session ends with a check.
concepts.scope: Mark which parts can shrink and which cannot. Protect the closing check.
concepts.example: Cutting a second demonstration to keep ten minutes for independent practice.

concepts.label: Formative assessment
concepts.def: Gathering evidence about learning in order to improve it while there is still time to act, by changing the teaching or giving the learner feedback.
concepts.scope: It earns the name only when the evidence is used. Collecting it and filing it is not formative.
concepts.example: Reading exit tickets and opening the next session by re-teaching the commonest error.
concepts.source: Black, P. and Wiliam, D. (1998) Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education, 5(1), pp. 7-74.

concepts.label: Summative assessment
concepts.def: Assessment that judges what a learner has achieved at the end of a period of learning, usually to grade or certify it.
concepts.scope: It should test the outcomes taught. Learners need to have met the task type in formative form first.
concepts.example: A marked essay at the end of a module.
concepts.source: Black, P. and Wiliam, D. (1998) Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education, 5(1), pp. 7-74.

concepts.label: Assessment criteria
concepts.def: The stated qualities that work must show to meet an outcome, written so that both learner and assessor can judge against them.
concepts.scope: Share criteria before the task. Describe quality in words learners can use, not only in grades.
concepts.example: A three-row rubric covering source choice, accuracy of citation and clarity of argument.
concepts.source: Sadler, D.R. (1989) Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18(2), pp. 119-144.

concepts.label: Feedback
concepts.def: Information that tells a learner how their current performance differs from the goal and what to do next, given in time for them to use it.
concepts.scope: Good feedback answers three questions: where am I going, how am I doing and where next. Comments the learner cannot act on are commentary, not feedback.
concepts.example: Your argument is clear but two claims lack sources. Add one source for each before you resubmit.
concepts.source: Hattie, J. and Timperley, H. (2007) The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1), pp. 81-112.

concepts.label: Evaluating teaching
concepts.def: Using evidence from learners, colleagues and your own records to judge how far the teaching helped learners reach the outcomes.
concepts.scope: Judge the teaching by learning evidence as well as by how learners felt. Satisfaction alone is a weak signal.
concepts.example: Reading end-of-session answers alongside a short learner survey and a colleague's notes.
concepts.source: Brookfield, S.D. (2017) Becoming a critically reflective teacher. 2nd edn. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

concepts.label: Peer observation
concepts.def: A colleague watches a session, or a recording, and gives you evidence about a focus you agreed beforehand.
concepts.scope: Agree a narrow focus first. Observers should describe what they saw before they judge it.
concepts.example: Asking a colleague to log how many learners answered each question you asked.
concepts.source: Brookfield, S.D. (2017) Becoming a critically reflective teacher. 2nd edn. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass.

concepts.label: Reflection-in-action
concepts.def: Noticing during a session that something is not working and changing course while you are still teaching.
concepts.scope: It depends on having clear intentions to notice against. A plan with outcomes makes mismatches visible.
concepts.example: Seeing blank looks, stopping and asking learners to explain the step to a neighbour.
concepts.source: Schön, D.A. (1983) The reflective practitioner: how professionals think in action. New York: Basic Books.

concepts.label: Reflection-on-action
concepts.def: Thinking about a session after it has finished to understand what happened and why, and to decide what to change.
concepts.scope: Do it soon, while you still remember details, and write it down. End with a decision.
concepts.example: Writing a short account of a session the same afternoon.
concepts.source: Schön, D.A. (1983) The reflective practitioner: how professionals think in action. New York: Basic Books.

concepts.label: Reflective cycle
concepts.def: A set sequence of prompts that guides reflection from what happened, through what it means, to what you will do differently.
concepts.scope: Pick one model and use it consistently. The prompts matter less than reaching a decision.
concepts.example: Working through description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan after a workshop.

concepts.label: Kolb cycle
concepts.def: A four-stage cycle of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation.
concepts.scope: Useful for seeing teaching as a loop. The stages overlap in practice.
concepts.example: Teaching a session, reviewing what happened, linking it to a principle and trying the change next week.
concepts.source: Kolb, D.A. (1984) Experiential learning. Englewood Cliffs: Prentice Hall.

concepts.label: Gibbs cycle
concepts.def: A six-stage reflective cycle: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion and action plan.
concepts.scope: Keep description separate from evaluation. The action plan is the point.
concepts.example: Describing exactly what happened in the practice task before judging it.
concepts.source: Gibbs, G. (1988) Learning by doing: a guide to teaching and learning methods. Oxford: Further Education Unit, Oxford Polytechnic.
